Short-term pre-aeration applied to the dry anaerobic digestion of MSW,
with a focus on the spectroscopic characteristics of dissolved organic
matter
Zhe Ni, Jianguo Liu ⇑, Mingwu Zhang
Key Laboratory for Solid Waste Management and Environment Safety, Ministry of Education of China, Tsinghua University, Beijing 10084, China
h i g h l i g h t s
 MSW with an 8-day pre-aeration produced the highest biogas yield of 192.4 NL/kg DM.
 Butyric acid dominated the VFAs (50–55%) in over acidifying reactors during dry AD.
 Accelerated protein degradation by pre-aeration neutralized excessive VFAs.
 Pre-aeration facilitated the conversion of protein- to fulvic- and humic-like matter.
 Fulvic- to protein-like ﬂuorescent matter ratio can evaluate the stability of dry AD.
a r t i c l e
i n f o

Municipal solid waste
Short-term pre-aeration
Dry anaerobic digestion
Methane production
Dissolved organic matter
Fluorescence excitation-emission matrix
(EEM) spectroscopy
a b s t r a c t
There is a growing trend toward considering municipal solid waste (MSW) with a large organic fraction as
a source of renewable energy using a dry anaerobic digestion (AD) process. Pre-aeration is effective in
improving the dry AD of MSW. However, due to a lack of information regarding the modiﬁcation of
organic components during pre-aeration and the relationship with the subsequent AD, the mechanisms
and optimum strength of this process remain unclear.
In this study, the role of different short-term pre-aeration durations (4, 8, and 14 days) in dry AD of
MSW was evaluated in batch-tests, with a focus on changes in the organic components during pre-
aeration and their impact on the subsequent spectral evolution of dissolved organic matter (DOM) and
bulk performance. Dry AD of MSW operated effectively after the 8-day pre-aeration. The accelerated
degradation of proteins during pre-aeration is critical for the subsequent AD, by reducing the organic
loading and providing a buffer for the ammonia generated. A favorable methanogenesis, facilitated by
pre-aeration, rapidly decreased protein-like ﬂuorescent matter by 2.8 times, by converting it to stable
humic- and fulvic-like groups. MSW with an 8-day pre-aeration produced the highest biogas yield
(192.4 NL/kg dry matter), representing 24.9% of the initial carbon recovered as methane. Excessive
pre-aeration of 14 days decreased the biogas yield by 33%. An insufﬁcient pre-aeration led to an exces-
sive butyric-type acidiﬁcation, with protein-like matter dominating the bulk DOM (81% of total ﬂuores-
cence intensity). Multivariate analysis methods conﬁrmed that spectroscopic indicators could evaluate
the stability of dry AD.

1. Introduction
The generation of municipal solid waste (MSW) in China has
increased due to rapid socioeconomic and population growth. It
has been reported that MSW collected in China amounted to
1.79 million tons in 2014 [1], with an estimated increment of
3–10% per year [2]. MSW generated in developing countries is
characterized by a high content of biodegradable organics and
moisture, with food waste usually accounting for more than 50%
by weight [3,4]. The improper processing and/or disposal of MSW
can have serious adverse effects on the surrounding environment.
However, the special chemical characteristics of MSW have gener-
ated interest in its use as a substrate for methane-rich gas via
anaerobic processes, such as dry/wet anaerobic digestion (AD) or
anaerobic bioreactor landﬁlling [5–8]. This could provide a solution

for the treatment of MSW together with the recovery of energy
from the biogas produced to respond to the challenge of global cli-
mate change.
A dry batch AD system is an important reactor type due to its
relative technical simplicity, the minimal capital cost and energy
consumption, and the limited requirements for waste pre-sorting
[9]. This process may be used as an in-vessel landﬁll, but with tem-
perature control and continuous leachate/percolate recirculation,
and little or no additional water, or sludge, needed be added to
the substrates [10]. However, the dry AD of raw MSW, especially
MSW with a large easily degradable fraction, may be especially
sensitive to the inhibition caused by excessive acidiﬁcation due
to organic overloading of the system. This will result in low oper-
ational stability and hinder the actual application [6,11,12]. To
overcome this problem, a large amount of inoculum or hydroxide
is usually applied in the early AD phase [8,10,13]. However, there
are disadvantages with these approaches because the efﬁciency
of the digester is decreased as some of the volume capacity is lost,
due to the presence of inoculum, and the salt content increases
dramatically in the digester.
Therefore, to improve the digestion performance in a dry AD
system (including MSW bioreactor landﬁlls), a short-term biologi-
cal pre-aeration (either in-situ or ex-situ aeration mode) prior to
anaerobic operation has received much interest in recent studies
[5,14–16]. The advantages of a short-term pre-aeration have
already been proven in the references mentioned above, and
include the rapid development of methanogenesis for energy recy-
cling and saving the volume capacity of digesters. Especially, the
process requires relatively little investment cost and process con-
trol is straightforward, which makes it particularly attractive for
developing countries [4]. Previous studies have suggested using
volatile solids (VS) (15%) and carbon losses (20–30%) as criteria
to determine the appropriate time to commence the subsequent
anaerobic operation [17,18]. However, the use of these parameters
is limited by the lack of information regarding the speciﬁc compo-
nents remaining after pre-aeration, where speciﬁc organic compo-
nents in waste signiﬁcantly inﬂuence its subsequent anaerobic
degradation behavior [7]. Due to the lack of a consistent aerobic
intensity, previous studies have neglected the underlying correla-
tions between the modiﬁcation of organic components during
the pre-aeration stage and its relationship with the subsequent
performance of AD, thereby limiting our understanding of the
potential application of this combined process.
Microorganisms only utilize organic matter when they are
dissolved in water. Most of the organic compounds in leachate
are present within the dissolved organic matter (DOM), including
dissolved components and the intermediates of microbial pro-
cesses during the degradation of organic matter, and can be used
to reﬂect the progress of the anaerobic process (e.g., the hydrolysis,
acidiﬁcation, and methanogenesis phases) [19,20]. Fluorescence
excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectroscopy provides a rapid
method to characterize the fractions of DOM in the liquid phase,
revealing the different types of ﬂuorescent materials, such as
protein-like, fulvic acid-like and humic acid-like substances [21].
Previous studies have demonstrated that this technique, with its
sensitivity and selective advantages, could be used to evaluate
the properties of water-extractable organic matter and/or DOM
during composting, landﬁlling, and AD processes, with respect to
various substrates [22–24]. However, to the best of our knowledge,
no study has been conducted to compare the distinction in spec-
troscopy characteristics during the dry AD of MSW with different
pre-aeration levels, and therefore this was the focus of this study.
The results will help to explain the degradation mechanisms of
pre-aerated MSW in a dry AD process, and thus enable a suitable
pre-aeration strength to be determined.
In this study, a series of short-term pre-aeration durations (0, 4,
8, and 14 days) were applied prior to the dry anaerobic degradation
of MSW in batch bioreactors. The novel aspect of this study was to
compare the effects of three different short-term pre-aeration time
periods on the modiﬁcation of organic components in waste, and
its relationship with subsequent AD with respect to the evolution
of liquid digestate and biogas generation. Fluorescence EEM spec-
troscopy coupled with parallel factor (PARAFAC) analysis was
applied to investigate the spectroscopic changes of DOM during
the AD process. Subsequently, a combination of a Pearson analysis
and principal component analysis (PCA) was used to evaluate the
inter-relationships between chemical and spectral indicators. The
results obtained above were used to discover the mechanisms
and potential application of short-term pre-aeration for enhancing
the dry AD of MSW.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate – synthetic MSW
Synthetic MSW was prepared in the lab to simulate the typical
composition of MSW generated in Beijing City [25]. In this way, the
discrepancy of substrate composition among the bioreactors was
minimized, allowing for more comparable results. The synthetic
MSW was prepared using a mixture (on a wet weight basis) of food
waste (63%), ofﬁce paper (13%), plastic (5%), and inorganic materi-
als, such as stones, glasses and metals (19%), respectively. The ini-
tial water content and biodegradable VS content of the synthetic
MSW were 57.5% (w/w) and 47.3% dry matter (DM), respectively.
The other chemical components and eluate characteristics from
the leaching test are shown in Table 1. Before loading into each
bioreactor, the synthetic MSW was manually shredded and well
mixed, with a uniform size of 20–40 mm.
2.2. Column experiments
2.2.1. Column equipment
Four laboratory-scale Plexiglas columns were used to compare
the effects of different short-term pre-aeration durations on the
dry AD of MSW. Each bioreactor had an internal diameter of
180 mm and a height of 320 mm. Detailed information regarding
the columns is provided elsewhere [26]. The bioreactor was
designed to allow operation under both aerobic and anaerobic
conditions by selectively switching the valves on or off. The oper-
ational temperature was kept constant at 35 ± 1 C through a
thermo-regulated insulation system, which covered the lateral
surfaces of the bioreactors.
2.2.2. Pre-aeration stage
Three kilos of MSW were loaded into each column, except the
control (AN bioreactor). While loading, approximately 150 g of
sludge compost (5% inoculation rate) was mixed in the waste to
enhance the aerobic degradation process. The short-term pre-
aeration duration was the sole variable. Three bioreactors were
operated with 4, 8, and 14 days pre-aeration, respectively, corre-
sponding to bioreactors R(4), R(8), and R(14). The initial airﬂow
rate was a preset cycle of 10 min aeration followed by a 20 min
pause, with an airﬂow rate of 0.5 L/min/kg waste. The headspace
gas composition before and after ventilation was measured. An
optimum oxygen level of 5–15% (v/v) was maintained by regulat-
ing the ventilation frequency during the whole pre-aeration phase.
Additionally, the leachate produced from each bioreactor was
drained daily and no leachate recirculation was applied during
the pre-aeration stage.

2.2.3. Dry batch AD stage
Destructive sampling was undertaken when each bioreactor
completed its designed pre-aeration term (i.e., 4, 8, and 14 days,
respectively). Approximately one tenth (w/w) of the pre-treated
waste was sampled using a sequential quartering procedure to
guarantee the homogeneity of later analyses. The remaining pre-
aerated waste was re-ﬁlled into an individual bioreactor. For the
AN bioreactor, only 2.5 kg of raw MSW was loaded, with no aerobic
compost or pre-aeration applied.
Anaerobically digested sludge, obtained from a full-scale AD
plant located in Beijing, was added as seeding material, accounting
for 10% (w/w) of the waste loaded in all of the bioreactors (i.e., AN,
R(4), R(8), and R(14)). The pH, total solids (TS), and VS of seeding
sludge were 7.8, 7.2% (w/w) and 46.5%TS, respectively. Addition-
ally, 200–250 mL of deionized water (10% weight of the loaded
waste) was introduced into each bioreactor for the moisture
content adjustment and initial leachate production. After these
operations, all of the bioreactors were subjected to anaerobic con-
ditions. The leachate generated from each bioreactor was manually
recirculated through a disperser in the top of the bioreactor every
2 days, and tested every 4 days throughout the whole anaerobic
period (100 days). The leachate withdrawn for analysis at each
sampling (25–30 mL) was replaced by an equivalent volume of
deionized water. The biogas generated was collected using 5 L
aluminum sampling bags and analyzed every 2 days.
2.3. Characterisation of spectroscopy
Fluorescence EEM spectroscopy was measured using a Hitachi
F-7000 ﬂuorescence spectrometer (Hitachi, Japan) at room temper-
ature according to He et al. [23], with minor modiﬁcations. The lea-
chate samples were ﬁltered through 0.45 lm membrane ﬁlters and
were preliminarily diluted to a TOC concentration of 5 mg/L
using deionized water. The slit widths were 5 nm for the excitation
and emission monochromators, and the scan speed was set to
12,000 nm/min. EEM spectra were gathered with the subsequent
scanning emission spectra (Em) from 240 to 600 nm at 1 nm incre-
ments by varying the excitation wavelength (Ex) from 220 to
450 nm at 5 nm increments. The leachate samples extracted from
the AD process in all runs on days 28, 56, and 84 were used for
EEM spectroscopy characterization. In addition, the ﬂuorescence
spectrum for ultrapure water was subtracted from the spectrum
of the sampled leachates to eliminate water Raman scattering
and reduce background noise.
All EEM spectral data were converted into excel format. A
PARAFAC analysis was then used to mathematically deconvolute
the original EEM spectral data into different independent groups
of ﬂuorescent components. This PARAFAC analysis was performed
using MATLAB software (ver. 7.0; MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
USA) with the DOMFluor toolbox (www.models.life.ku.dk), in
accordance with previous reports [23,24,27]. In detail, after several
post-acquisition steps (i.e., removal of scattering and data arrange-
ment) to correct the ﬂuorescence EEM spectra, a series of PARAFAC
models with two to seven components were ﬁtted to the test data.
A split half analysis (Fig. S1) and residual analysis (Fig. S2) were
used to identify the correct number of components. The concentra-
tion scores of the PARAFAC components were normalized to the
Raman peak area (R.U.) and expressed as the maximum ﬂuores-
cence intensity (Fmax).
2.4. Other analytical methods
The physical and chemical characteristics of the solid samples
before and after pre-aeration were measured. The moisture con-
tent was determined by heating the solid samples at 105 C. The
VS content was determined by ashing the dry samples, after the
removal of plastics, at 550 C to a constant weight in a mufﬂe fur-
nace. Preliminary dried and shredded solid samples (granule scale
less than 1 mm) were used to analyze their organic components.
Elemental analysis was undertaken using a carbon-hydrogen-
nitrogen analyzer (model CE 440; EAI, Oakland, NJ, USA). Proteins,
lipids, and lignocellulose content were determined according to a
method used in a previous study [28]. The carbohydrate content
was calculated by subtracting the sum of lipids, proteins, and lig-
nocellulose content from the VS.
The waste eluates were obtained by the water extraction of pre-
dried and ground waste, shaken for 24 h in ultrapure water (1:10
ratio of solid/liquid w/w) at room temperature. Liquid samples,
both from waste eluates and anaerobic leachate, were centrifuged
at 10,000 for 10 min and ﬁltered through 0.45 lm membrane
ﬁlters. The ﬁltrate was tested for pH, dissolved organic carbon
(DOC),
alkalinity,
soluble
chemical
oxygen
demand
(SCOD),
NH4
+-N, and VFAs according to APHA methods [29]. The concentra-
tions of DOC and VFA were measured using a total organic carbon
analyzer (TOC-Vcph, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) and gas chromatog-
raphy equipped with a ﬂame ionization detector (GC-2014,
Shimadzu), respectively. SUVA254 values (reported in L/mg/m)
were determined by dividing the UV–Vis absorbance measured at
k = 254 nm by the TOC concentration [20].
The O2 emissions during the short-term pre-aeration and the
biogas produced during the AD process (mainly CH4 and CO2) were
measured by gas chromatography using a thermal conductivity
detector (GC-2014, Shimadzu).
All analyses of solid, liquid, and gas samples were conducted in
duplicate.

2.5. Statistical methods
PCA was conducted to analyze the correlations between chem-
ical and spectroscopic indicators in anaerobic leachate based on
their correlation matrix, with a dataset normalized by taking the
log10, extracting the mean, and dividing it by the standard devia-
tion. PCA was performed using CANOCO for Windows software
(ver. 4.5; Biometris, Wageningen, Netherlands).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Characterization of pre-aerated waste
The characteristics of the solid phase and eluate of the initial
and pre-aerated waste are given in Table 1.
The pre-aeration process clearly altered the VS content and
fractional content of organic components in substrates. The VS
content in solid waste decreased by 10.6, 29.2, and 47.6% (based
on dry weight) after 4, 8, and 14 days pre-aeration, respectively.
Carbohydrates contributed to most of the VS losses during this pro-
cess, ranging from 29.2 to 52% across the different pre-aeration
durations. A clear decrease in the fractional content of proteins
was observed between the R(4) and (R8) bioreactors, suggesting
that the organic nitrogen degradation mainly occurred over days
5–8, which corresponded to the thermophilic period during the
pre-aeration process (average 51.6 C). In contrast, the relative
fraction content of lignocelluloses increased from the initial value
of 0.363 g/g TS to 0.389 and 0.400 g/g TS in the R(8) and R
(14) bioreactors, respectively. This could be explained by the
slower degradation rate and special microorganism metabolism
pathways required compared with other organic components as
reported by Zhang et al. [30], who concluded that inoculation
and a sufﬁcient incubation time were indispensable for lignocellu-
lose disintegration and degradation. These ﬁndings showed that
the degradation of different organic components in waste during
the pre-aeration stage was not synchronous.
The results of the leaching test on solid samples revealed signif-
icant discrepancies in all parameters. Higher pH values were
observed in the samples from bioreactors R(8) and R(14), which
were consistent with the lower values of the VFA to alkalinity ratio.
The NH4
+-N concentration increased as the pre-aeration duration
was prolonged, while the DOC and VFA concentrations in the
leachate extracted from the solid sample in R(4) were clearly
higher than those obtained for the other indicators, largely due to
the
enhanced

low-intensity pre-aeration process [31]. Consequently, the pre-
aeration periods of 8 and 14 days resulted in decreased DOC and
VFA concentrations in the eluate of solid wastes, which was attrib-
uted to the ﬁnal degradation of easily biodegradable organic mat-
ter, especially carbohydrates and proteins (Table 1). He et al. [32]
reported that the DOC of MSW excavated from an actual landﬁll
is usually less than 1.0 g/kg waste, which is clearly much lower than
the result obtained even for the 14-day pre-aerated waste in this
present study (26.9 g/kg waste). These results suggested that even
after short-term pre-aeration (e.g., 4–14 days) the wastes were still
unstable in terms of DOC.
SUVA254 is an indicator that indirectly reﬂects the degree of bio-
logical degradability of the samples. The SUVA254 values were
increased by 3 times following 8 and 14 days pre-aeration. Shao
et al. [33] observed that the SUVA254 values of water extracts of
MSWs after the hydrolysis-aerobic process (100 days) were around
3.0 L/mg/m, which was clearly higher than the values from short-
term pre-aerated waste in this study, implying a lack of biological
stabilization of pre-treated substrates. This ﬁnding was consistent
with the results for the DOC concentration.
3.2. Bulk characterization of pH, SCOD, NH4
+-N, VFAs and biogas
production during the AD process
The anaerobic phase was operated for a period of around
100 days. Leachate NH4
+-N, pH, and SCOD concentrations obtained
on speciﬁc days during the anaerobic landﬁlling process are shown
in Fig. S3. The pH increased in all runs, which could be attributed to
the alkaline yield due to the mineralization of proteinaceous mate-
rials. A higher pH was observed in bioreactors R(8) and R(14), with
ﬁnal values of 8.2 and 7.9, respectively, at the end of study. The pH
of bioreactors AN and R(4) (6.0) was below the optimum value
for methane production throughout the whole experimental per-
iod [6,12]. Additionally, pre-aeration clearly increased the initial
NH4
+-N concentration in leachates (samples on day 4 from bioreac-
tors R(4), R(8), and R(14)), which corresponded to the higher initial
pH values in individual bioreactors. This result suggested that the
increased ammonia levels obtained by pre-aeration could neutral-
ize the VFAs generated during anaerobic treatment, which is
beneﬁcial for the development of methanogenesis conditions.
The longer the duration of pre-aeration, the lower the ﬁnal
NH4
+-N concentration that was observed. The lower SCOD for biore-
actors R(8) to R(14) suggested that the successful conversion of
DOM in leachates was achieved by an 8 and 14 day pre-aeration,
with SCOD removal efﬁciencies of 90.3 and 83.2% at the end of
the experiment, respectively. In contrast, the low removal efﬁcien-
cies of SCOD in the AN and R(4) bioreactors implied that the DOM
in leachates was still unstable.
The changes in the VFA content during the AD process in all
runs are presented in Fig. 1. An obvious accumulation of VFAs
was observed in the AN and R(4) bioreactors throughout the whole
experimental period, with similar chemical proﬁles mainly consist-
ing of butyric acid (50–55%), followed by acetic acid (17–25%) and
propionic acid (5–10%), which was typically butyric-type acidiﬁca-
tion [34]. At the end of study (on day 100), the total VFA content in
terms of COD were 32,000 and 39,000 mg/L in AN and R(4),
respectively. These results implied that the reactors remained in
the acidogenesis phase. However, the VFA concentrations in biore-
actors R(8) and R(14) decreased rapidly after the initial peak on day
12. Only acetic acid was detected in the ﬁnal samples, and the
average content was less than 20 mg/L, which represents a high
AD efﬁciency.
The biogas production from the AN, R(4), R(8), and R(14) biore-
actors during the dry AD process is shown in Fig. S4. There were
considerable changes in biogas yield among the bioreactors with
the different pre-aeration durations. In bioreactors R(8) and R
(14), after the short start-up period (8 days), methane was the
main component in the biogases generated, being present mostly
in the range of 50–68%. The accumulated biogas production from
bioreactors R(8) and R(14) was 192.4 and 151.6 NL/kg DM, with
an average methane content of 56.1 and 55.1% (v/v), respectively.
The generation of biogas was almost completed within 54–62 days,
suggesting
that
an
accelerated
stabilization
processes
was
achieved through an 8- and 14-day pre-aeration. In contrast, there
was almost no methane (average content <0.2%, v/v) generated in
the AN bioreactor, which was attributable to the excessive acidiﬁ-
cation, generating only a small amount of biogas consisting of
mainly CO2 and H2. In the R(4) bioreactor, the accumulated biogas
production was 25.0 NL/kg DM at the end of the experimental per-
iod. Methane was detected >40% (40.1%, v/v) for the ﬁrst time
after an anaerobic cultivation of 88 days. Xu et al. [12] reported
that methane content greater than 40% is required for the biogas
to be technically or economically feasible. This showed that a very
long lag-phase occurred in R(4) bioreactor, implying that there was
still an overload of organic matter after 4 days of pre-aeration.
All of the regular indicators detected above were in a reasonable
range for the anaerobic degradation of real MSW [5,6].

3.3. Carbon mass balance combining pre-aeration and AD process
The carbon conversion was evaluated throughout the whole
experimental period in all of the bioreactors (Table 2). The analysis
was conducted following a method reported by Zhang et al. [35].
The distribution of carbon mass was distinctly different among
the bioreactors with different pre-aeration durations. As the pre-
aeration duration increased, more organic carbon was converted
into the gas phase as CO2 during this stage (7.6–51.0%), while the
carbon released via leachate slightly changed (4.5–7.7%). When con-
sidering the combined process, the maximum conversion of carbon
into methane (24.9%) was observed in bioreactor R(8), in which the
raw waste was pre-aerated for 8 days. The excessive pre-aeration
used in bioreactor R(14) further consumed the organic carbon in

decrease of 33%. The ﬁnal mass of carbon in solid residuals and
leachate was almost the same from bioreactors R(8) and R(14),
implying the complete stabilization of organic carbon in these
bioreactors. On the other hand, for the AN and R(4) bioreactors, only
15.6 and 19.4% of the initial carbon was released throughout the
whole experiment period, respectively, mainly as CO2 and DOM in
leachate. Therefore, 70% of the initial mass of carbon was left in
the solid residues, indicating a very low efﬁciency of organic miner-
alization. In conclusions, when considering energy recovery, the
duration of pre-aeration prior to anaerobic operation should be
around 8 days for MSW with a high organic fraction.
3.4. Spectroscopic characterization of DOM during the AD process
3.4.1. Fluorescence EEM spectroscopy
Fluorescence EEM spectroscopy was used to characterize the
DOM in leachates from all of the bioreactors and their spectroscopy
priorities over time (i.e., 28-, 56-, and 84-day samples, respec-
tively) are shown in Fig. S5.
According to Chen et al. [21], EEM spectroscopy can be used for
the analysis of ﬁve regions using consistent excitation and emis-
sion wavelength boundaries. A total of ﬁve distinct peaks were
directly observed during the whole AD process in all runs. Peaks
A, B, and C were located in Ex/Em wavelengths of 275/298–310,
275/338–342 and 220–225/305–312 nm, respectively. Both peaks
A and B were microbial by-products (i.e., tyrosine- and protein-
like, and tryptophan- and
protein-like), while, peak
C was
associated with tyrosine-like materials as free molecules or bound
to amino acids and proteins [32]. Peaks D and E are located in
Ex/Em wavelengths of 336/430 nm and 280/430 nm, respectively.
Previous studies have implied that these two peaks were both
attributable to humic-like organic substances [21]. In general,
tyrosine-like and tryptophan-like materials are considered to be
easily biodegradable substrates [22,33], while continuous mineral-
ization, re-polymerization, and condensation pathways from low-
weight molecules or the degradation of lignin lead to the formation
of humic-like organic substances, which are effective indicators of
organic matter stabilization [23,24].
The spectra obtained from bioreactors AN and R(4) were very
similar. Only peaks A, B, and C were directly observed during the
whole experimental period (i.e., 28, 56, 84-day samples). These
peaks were also found in young leachate sources in a previous
study [36]. In bioreactors R(8) and R(14) peaks A, B, and C almost
vanished as anaerobic landﬁlling progressed, while peaks D and E
were visually enhanced as anaerobic degradation proceeded
(i.e., 56 and 84-day samples), suggesting the stabilization of
organic matter in the leachate. The ﬂuorescence EEM spectroscopy
results were consistent with the previous results for the bulk char-
acteristics of leachates and biogases in individual bioreactors
(Figs. 2, S3 and S4).
3.4.2. Characterization of EEM-PAPAFAC
To acquire more useful information on the evolution of the
chemically relevant ﬂuorescent components in DOM, a PAPAFAC
analysis was conducted using the raw EEM spectra. The inspection
results (Figs. S1 and S2) and visual recognition (Fig. 2) conﬁrmed
that the ﬁve-component model was suitable for characterizing
the DOM extracted from the leachate during the AD process. The
maximum Ex/Em wavelength of component C1 was the same as
peaks D and E in the raw EEM spectroscopy results, while, that of
component C2 was consistent with the raw peaks A and C
(Fig. S5). This proved that components C1 and C2 were humic-like
and protein-like substances, respectively. Component C3 had two
excitation peaks at 225 and 285 nm, with an emission maximum
at 385. Zheng et al. [20] indicated that peaks at the Ex/Em wave-
length of 230 and 290/390 nm could be attributed to fulvic acid-
like components, and therefore C3 was considered to be similar to
fulvic
acid-like
components.
Components
C4
(Ex/Em
wave-
length = 250 and 275/440 nm) and C5 (Ex/Em wavelength = 235
and 330/425 nm) had similar ﬂuorescence positions. Compared
with component C5, the primary ﬂuorescence peak for component
C4 was red shifted, with longer wavelengths attributed to the
increase of carbonyl, hydroxyl, alkoxyl, and amino groups in ﬂuo-
rophores [37,38]. Thus, C4 was considered to be similar to fulvic
acid-like compounds, while C5 was ascribed to humic-like organic
substances [21]. The results of the PARAFAC analysis not only con-
ﬁrmed the previous ﬁndings through the direct visual identiﬁcation
of peaks in the raw EEM spectroscopy (components C1 and C2), but
also revealed some new peaks which were previously unidentiﬁed
(components C3, C4, and C5).
3.4.3. Evaluation of spectra changes during AD process
The changes of the concentration scores of the PARAFAC compo-
nents (Fmax) reﬂect the conformation of the ﬂuorescence compo-
nents under the different states of AD [23,38]. In this study, the
changes of the PARAFAC components, especially component C2,
could be used to categorize all of the samples into two groups
(Fig. 3(a) and (b)). The Fmax values (0.20–0.26 R.U.) and the relative
percentage (>81%) of component C2 from bioreactors AN and R(4)
were relatively stable during the whole AD process. In contrast, in
the samples from bioreactors R(8) and R(14) there was a clear
decrease in the C2 values as AD proceeded, with an average reduc-
tion of 2.8 times from the 28 to 84-d samples; meanwhile, for com-
ponents C1, C4, and C5 there was a signiﬁcant increase over time.
These ﬁndings implied that excessive acidiﬁcation tended to result
in a ﬂuorescence peak associated with protein-like matter in lea-
chate. In contrast, a favorable AD process can efﬁciently decompose
protein-like substances, while converting them into more stable
fulvic and humic substances.

to that of protein-like matter can be used to determine the

3.6. Implications for pre-aeration prior to anaerobic treatment
Theoretically, a favorable methanogenic condition should bal-
ance the hydrolytic, acetogenic, and methanogenic activities and
avoid potential inhibitions [10,11]. However, a dry anaerobic batch
system ﬁlled with raw MSW with a large organic fraction usually
suffers from excessive acidiﬁcation due to the overload of organic
matter, and therefore fails to establish a favorable methanogenesis.
In this study, the organic loading in bioreactor AN was up to
84 g VS/L, which is very high even for an AD with sufﬁcient addi-
tion of inoculum [39]. Proteins and carbohydrates are considered
to be the most easily hydrolyzed and acidiﬁed substrates during
a typical AD process [20]. Pre-aeration for 4 days in bioreactor R
(4) achieved a level of 10.6% VS (accompanied by 12.1% carbon)
and carbohydrate losses of 46.7%, but it had no obvious effect on
relieving the excessive acidiﬁcation and long lag-phase in the sub-
sequent dry AD process (Figs. 1, S3 and S4). This could be explained

by the 4-day pre-aeration only removing 6.6% of proteins during
this time period, and therefore the majority of the protein content
remained in the pre-treated waste. Moreover, EEM data for the AN
and R(4) bioreactors showed that the accumulation of protein-like
matter (component C2), which originated from the hydrolysis of
the remaining proteins in aerobically pre-treated waste, occurred
during the experimental period. Li et al. [24] reported that the
tyrosine-like group in leachate that accumulated over time might
become an inhibitory factor for converting organic matter to bio-
gas. The accumulation of this group could hamper the hydrolysis
of other organic polymers in the waste, resulting in the failure of
the AD system.
The 8-day pre-aeration resulted in proteins losses of 50.2%,
with an accompanying carbohydrate removal of 78.8%. Therefore,
the organic loading in R(8) dropped to 62 g VS/L. Although this
organic loading is still high during a typical AD process, no obvious
inhibitions, as
illustrated by
the
leachate parameters,
were
observed in bioreactor R(8), and its accumulated methane produc-
tion reached 107.7 NL/kg DM. One possible cause of this, as
observed in the initial leachate from bioreactor R(8), might be
the presence of a suitable NH4
+-N concentration at the beginning
of the dry digestion process (Fig. S3). Zhai et al. [40] reported that
an important factor impacting on pH was the NH4
+-N concentration,
which acts as a buffer under high VFA conditions in anaerobic lea-
chate. Generally, the ammoniﬁcation process is slow in a typical
AD process [6,12], and therefore the unbalanced degradation rates
of organic carbon and organic nitrogen tend to constrain microbial
activity due to the lack of sufﬁcient nutrition and the very low pH
conditions in the liquid phase. In contrast, the degradation of
organic nitrogen under aerobic conditions is much easier due to
there being fewer limiting factors [41]. From this perspective, it
could be concluded that suitable pre-aeration is capable of enhanc-
ing the ammoniation process of organic nitrogen in waste before
anaerobic conditions arise, while the higher NH4
+-N concentration
in leachate could neutralize the excessive VFAs generated in the
digesters to maintain an ideal pH for methanogenesis.
Based on the observations reported above, biological short-term
pre-aeration could result in a different order of degradation of
organic components in waste. Compared with carbohydrates,
proteins are more resistant to aerobic biodegradation during this
process and require a longer time to decompose. The degraded pro-
teins could provide a certain amount of buffer capacity, and
enhance the start-up of a subsequent dry AD. Therefore, the accel-
erated degradation of proteins in waste by pre-aeration is the most
important mechanism that strengthens AD in a dry batch system.
Previous studies [6,12] considered the use of pH values (6.5–8.0)
and the VFA concentration (<6400 mg/L, in terms of COD) as mon-
itoring parameters to determine the optimum switching point
between in-situ aerobic pretreatment and anaerobic operation.
Regarding the ex-situ pre-aeration process prior to anaerobic treat-
ment (e.g., landﬁlling or dry AD), according to this study, a possible
strategy for determining the switching point is to monitor the
degree of degradation of proteins in waste, which is more reason-
able for the avoidance of excessive pre-aeration than the use of
bulk characteristics (e.g., VS and carbon losses) that have been
reported in previous studies [17,18]. However, further experiments
are needed to determine the optimum degree of proteins degrada-
tion to enhance methane production from the dry AD of MSW and
reduce pre-treatment costs.
4. Conclusions
Short-term pre-aeration signiﬁcantly improved the anaerobic
degradation of MSW with a high organic fraction in a dry AD pro-
cess. The accelerated degradation of proteins in waste by pre-
aeration was a key factor in enhancing the start-up of a dry AD pro-
cess. On one hand, protein degradation reduced the organic loading
in a system, whereas on the other hand the ammonia generated
provided a buffer to neutralize the excessive VFAs produced during
the dry AD process. MSW with an 8-day pre-aeration obtained the
highest biogas yield of 192.4 NL/kg DM, with an average methane
content of 56.1% (v/v). This result represented a recovery of
24.9% of the initial carbon in waste as methane during the inte-
grated process of an 8-day pre-aeration and dry AD. When the
pre-aeration was extended to 14 days, the cumulative biogas yield
was 33% lower than the 8-day pre-aeration due to the excessive
organic matter consumption. To avoid excessive pre-aeration, it is
advisable to interrupt the pre-aeration process based on the degree
of proteins degradation and commence the subsequent anaerobic
operation. Further investigation is needed to optimize this param-
eter by regulating pre-aeration modes.
In comparison, insufﬁcient pre-aeration resulted in excessive
butyrate-type acid inhibition during AD, with an accumulation of
ﬂuorescence components related to protein-like matter. Therefore,
the response in the spectral properties of DOM (e.g., the relative
abundance of C2 and the C4/C2 ratio) to the different reactor con-
ditions indicates that these parameters can be used to identify pro-
cess stability during the dry AD of MSW.
